{{nihongo|'''Umamioka Watamuki Shrine'''|馬見岡綿向神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Ōmi Province]].

'''Umamioka Watamuki Shrine''' (うまみおかわたむきじんじゃ) is the satomiya (village shrine) of Ōtake Shrine, which is enshrined on the summit of {{ill|Mount Watamuki|Q11607423|qid=Q11607423}} towering to the east of {{ill|Hino, Shiga|Q1208020|qid=Q1208020|lt=Hino Town}}, {{ill|Gamō District, Shiga|Q931658|qid=Q931658}}, {{ill|Shiga Prefecture|ace|Prefektur Shiga|af|Shiga-prefektuur|an|Prefectura de Shiga|ar|شيغا (محافظة)|az|Şiqa prefekturası|azb|شیقا اوستانی|ban|Préféktur Shiga|be|Сіга (прэфектура)|bg|Шига|bn|শিগা প্রশাসনিক অঞ্চল|br|Prefedelezh Shiga|ca|Prefectura de Shiga|cdo|Shiga-gâing|ce|Сига (префектура)|ceb|Shiga-ken|ckb|پارێزگای شیگا|cs|Prefektura Šiga|cy|Shiga (talaith)|da|Shiga-præfekturet|de|Präfektur Shiga|eo|Gubernio Ŝiga|es|Prefectura de Shiga|et|Shiga prefektuur|eu|Shiga (prefektura)|fa|استان شیگا|fi|Shigan prefektuuri|fr|Préfecture de Shiga|frr|Shiga (Prefektüür)|ga|Maoracht Shiga|gl|Prefectura de Shiga|hak|Shiga-yen|he|שיגה (מחוז)|hr|Shiga (prefektura)|hu|Siga prefektúra|hy|Սիգա (պրեֆեկտուրա)|id|Prefektur Shiga|ilo|Prepektura ti Shiga|it|Prefettura di Shiga|ja|滋賀県|jv|Préfèktur Shiga|ka|სიგის პრეფექტურა|ko|시가현|la|Shigaënsis|lt|Šigos prefektūra|lv|Sigas prefektūra|mk|Шига (префектура)|mn|Шига муж|mni|ꯁꯤꯒꯥ ꯂꯝꯈꯥꯢ|mr|शिगा प्रांत|ms|Wilayah Shiga|ne|सिगा|nl|Shiga (prefectuur)|no|Shiga (prefektur)|os|Сигæ|pl|Prefektura Shiga|pnb|ضلع شیگا|pt|Shiga|ro|Prefectura Shiga|ru|Сига|sco|Shiga Prefectur|se|Shiga prefektuvra|sh|Prefektura Shiga|si|ෂිගා ප්‍රාන්තය|simple|Shiga Prefecture|sk|Šiga (prefektúra)|sr|Префектура Шига|su|Préféktur Shiga|sv|Shiga prefektur|sw|Mkoa wa Shiga|tg|Устони Шига|th|จังหวัดชิงะ|tl|Prepektura ng Shiga|tr|Shiga|tt|Сига (префектура)|uk|Префектура Сіґа|ur|شیگا پریفیکچر|vi|Shiga|war|Shiga (prefektura)|wuu|滋贺县|zh|滋贺县|zh_classical|滋賀縣|zh_min_nan|Siga-koān|zh_yue|滋賀縣|qid=Q131358}}. It is identified with the {{ill|Shikinaisha|lt=Shikinaisha|qid=Q134917286}} Umamioka Shrine {{Sfn|Hino Town History Editorial Committee|2013|p=294}}. Its former shrine rank was {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Prefectural Shrine}}. Every year on May 2 and 3, the {{ill|Hino Matsuri|Q111034300|qid=Q111034300}} is held as the annual festival.

=== Enshrined Deities ===
Mount Watamuki is regarded as the sacred mountain, and three Izumo-related deities are enshrined {{Sfn|Heibonsha Regional Data Center|1991|pp=503–504}}{{Efn|It is said that many people of Izumo lineage lived around the shrine, and the irrigation canal that serves as the water source for rice cultivation is also called the “Izumo River.” {{Sfn|Heibonsha Regional Data Center|1991|p=504}}}}.
* {{ill|Ame no Hohi|qid=Q10940685|lt=Ame-no-Hohi-no-Mikoto}} (Amenohohi-no-Mikoto)
* {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Ame-no-Hinadore-no-Mikoto}} (Amenohinadore-no-Mikoto)
* Takemikumao-ushi-no-Mikoto (Takemikumao-ōshi-no-Mikoto)

=== History ===
According to tradition, during the time of {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|ar|الإمبراطور جينمو|arz|الامبراطور جينمو|as|জিম্মু|az|Cimmu|bcl|Emperador Jimmu|be|Імператар Дзіму|ca|Jinmu|cdo|Sìng-ū Tiĕng-huòng|ckb|ئیمپراتۆر جینمو|cs|Džimmu|de|Jimmu|el|Αυτοκράτορας Τζίμου|eo|Imperiestro Jinmu|es|Jinmu Tennō|et|Jimmu|eu|Jimmu enperadorea|fa|امپراتور جینمو|fi|Jinmu|fr|Jinmu|hak|Sṳ̀n-vú Thiên-fòng|he|ג'ימו, קיסר יפן|hi|सम्राट जिममु|hr|Jinmu|hu|Dzsinmu japán császár|id|Jimmu|it|Jinmu|ja|神武天皇|jv|Jimmu Tenno|ka|ძიმუ|ko|진무 천황|kw|Emperour Jimmu|la|Jimmu|lt|Imperatorius Džinmu|lv|Džimmu|mn|Эзэн Хаан Жиммү|mr|जिम्मू|ms|Maharaja Jimmu|my|ဂျင်းမူ ဧကရာဇ်|nl|Jimmu|no|Jimmu|pl|Jimmu|pt|Jimmu|ru|Император Дзимму|sh|Car Jimmu|simple|Emperor Jimmu|sl|Cesar Džinmu|sr|Џинму|sv|Jimmu|th|จักรพรรดิจิมมุ|tl|Emperador Jimmu|tr|Jimmu|uk|Імператор Дзімму|uz|Jimmu|vi|Thiên hoàng Jimmu|war|Emperador Jimmu|wuu|神武天皇|zh|神武天皇|zh_classical|神武天皇|zh_min_nan|Sîn-bú Thian-hông|zh_yue|神武天皇|qid=Q200188}}, a pioneer deity from {{ill|Izumo Province|Q582846|qid=Q582846}} was invited and enshrined, and in 545 (Year 6 of Emperor Kinmei), a shrine was built on the summit of {{ill|Mount Watamuki|Q11607423|qid=Q11607423}}, marking the beginning of the shrine. In 796 (Year 15 of Enryaku) in the early Heian period, it is said to have been relocated to its present site.<ref>{{Cite web|Japanese|url=http://guide.jr-odekake.net/spot/1003 |title=Umamioka Watamuki Shrine - Kinki Area | Odekake Guide: JR Odekake Net |publisher=West Japan Railway Company |accessdate=March 7, 2018}}</ref> In the medieval period, in 1209 (Year 3 of Shōgen), a fire destroyed all the shrine buildings, but reconstruction did not occur until 181 years later, in 1390 (Year 1 of Meitoku) {{Sfn|Hino Town History Editorial Committee|2009|p=164}}.

=== Patronage of the Gamō Clan ===
In the late medieval period, the {{ill|Gamō clan|Q2975251|qid=Q2975251}}, who built a castle town in Hino, patronized the shrine as their clan shrine, and it gained reverence as the general shrine of Upper Gamō District.<ref name="日野観光協会"/> The shrine buildings, which had burned down in warfare in 1521 (Year 2 of Daiei), were repaired in 1549 (Year 18 of Tenmon) by {{ill|Gamō Sadahide|Q5368466|qid=Q5368466}} and in 1571 (Year 2 of Genki) by {{ill|Gamō Katahide|Q842016|qid=Q842016}} {{Sfn|Hino Town History Editorial Committee|2013|p=298}}. In addition, in 1557 (Year 3 of Kōji), Gamō Sadahide commissioned three new mikoshi (portable shrines) and participated in the festival procession accompanied by offerings and local samurai from 128 villages under Gamō control {{Sfn|Heibonsha Regional Data Center|1991|p=504}}. {{ill|Gamō Ujisato|Q906580|qid=Q906580}} moved to Ise in 1584 (Year 12 of Tenshō) and later to Aizu, but continued making donations to this shrine {{Sfn|Heibonsha Regional Data Center|1991|p=504}}. When he was transferred to Aizu-Kurokawa, he is said to have renamed the new domain “{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Aizuwakamatsu}}” in memory of the pine grove called “Wakamatsu no Mori” that once stood along the approach to this shrine.<ref name="日野町"/> After Ujisato, the Gamō lineage continued through {{ill|Gamō Hideyuki|Q5520435|qid=Q5520435|lt=Hideyuki}}, {{ill|Gamō Tadasato|Q8513818|qid=Q8513818|lt=Tadayoshi}}, and {{ill|Gamō Tadatomo|Q8513824|qid=Q8513824|lt=Tadachika}}, and although their domains were transferred successively from Aizu to Utsunomiya, Aizu, and Matsuyama, donations to Watamuki Shrine continued {{Sfn|Heibonsha Regional Data Center|1991|p=504}}. However, in 1634 (Year 11 of Kan’ei), Gamō Tadachika, then lord of Iyo Matsuyama Domain, died without an heir, leading to the extinction of the Gamō family, and patronage from the clan ceased {{Sfn|Hino Town History Editorial Committee|2013|pp=298–299}}.

=== Worship by Ōmi-Hino Merchants ===
In the early modern period, {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Ōmi-Hino merchants}} ({{ill|Ōmi merchant|Q11638475|qid=Q11638475}}) revered the shrine as a deity of success and good fortune. The worship hall, ema hall, stone lanterns, stone bridges, and other structures donated by these merchants remain within the precincts.<ref name="日野観光協会">{{Cite web|Japanese|url=https://www.hino-kanko.jp/sight/umamioka/ |title=Umamioka Watamuki Shrine |publisher=Hino Tourism Association |accessdate=2022-03-11}}</ref> The semicircular stone bridge over which the mikoshi pass during the {{ill|Hino Matsuri|Q111034300|qid=Q111034300}} was completed in 1681 (Year 9 of Enpō) through donations from Ōmi-Hino merchants {{Sfn|Hino Town History Editorial Committee|2007|pp=433–434}}. In 1708 (Year 5 of Hōei), the current main hall was completed through widespread public fundraising {{Sfn|Hino Town History Editorial Committee|2013|p=299}}{{Sfn|Hino Town History Editorial Committee|2007|p=377}}. The Nakaigenzaemon family of Hino townspeople, particularly the father-and-son pair Ryōyū and Mitsumasa, were especially devoted; they repaired the kagura hall in 1782 (Year 2 of Tenmei) and completed the worship hall in 1803 (Year 3 of Kyōwa) {{Sfn|Hino Town History Editorial Committee|2013|pp=299–300}}. In addition to the shrine buildings, 19 festival floats (16 of which remain today) that adorn the Hino Festival were completed from the early 18th century through the financial power of Hino townspeople {{Sfn|Heibonsha Regional Data Center|1991|p=504}}.

=== Lodging of Prince Asaka Yasuhiko ===
When the imperial family member {{ill|Prince Yasuhiko Asaka|Q701503|qid=Q701503}} was scheduled to visit Hino Town on military duty in October 1929 (Shōwa 4), the shrine office was selected as his lodging. However, since the office had just been completed and lacked bathing facilities, and construction of fences and other features was necessary, facilities such as a “bath exclusively for His Highness” were newly installed {{Sfn|Hino Town Shiga Prefecture Education Association|1930|p=245}}.

Prince Asaka arrived at 3:00 p.m. on October 24 and immediately paid a visit to the shrine. On the 25th, after visits to {{ill|Hino Elementary School|Q21654310|qid=Q21654310|lt=Hino Elementary School}} and {{ill|Hino Girls’ High School|Q11564656|qid=Q11564656|lt=Hino Girls’ High School}}, he personally planted a pine tree in front of the shrine office as a commemorative tree, and departed on the morning of the 26th {{Sfn|Hino Town Shiga Prefecture Education Association|1930|p=245}}.

Public Transportation
* From {{ill|Ōmi-Hachiman Station|Q1042782|qid=Q1042782}} on the {{ill|Tōkaidō Main Line|Q1190152|qid=Q1190152}} ({{ill|Biwako Line|Q804135|qid=Q804135}}) of {{ill|West Japan Railway Company|Q502125|qid=Q502125|lt=JR}} or the {{ill|Ohmi Railway Yōkaichi Line|Q7081107|qid=Q7081107}} (Manyō Akane Line), or from {{ill|Hino Station (Shiga)|Q5767373|qid=Q5767373|lt=Hino Station}} on the {{ill|Ohmi Railway Main Line|Q7081104|qid=Q7081104}} (Minakuchi–Gamōno Line). Take the {{ill|Ohmi Railway Bus|Q129172682|qid=Q129172682}} bound for Kitahataguchi, get off at Mukōmachi stop, then walk about 3 minutes.
By Car
* About 20 minutes from {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Yōkaichi IC}} on the {{ill|Meishin Expressway|Q904481|qid=Q904481}}.
* About 20 minutes from {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Kōka-Tsuchiyama IC}} on the {{ill|Shin-Meishin Expressway|Q7497118|qid=Q7497118}}.
